intro.en: How a child with breathing difficulty is examined, from history and chest inspection to tapping, listening and reading the signs.

items.summary: A short history plus a look inside the nose, over the face sinuses and at the throat before the chest itself is examined.

blocks.title: History prompts
bullets: Ask about runny nose, nosebleeds, snoring and breathing through the mouth.
Ask about pain or heaviness over the cheeks and forehead, which hints at sinus trouble.
Ask about sore throat, pain on swallowing and past tonsil infections.

blocks.title: Upper airway check
bullets: Look into each nostril for discharge, bleeding, a bent midline partition or swollen fleshy ridges.
Press over the cheek and forehead hollows and note any tenderness there.
Inspect the tonsils, throat wall and mouth for redness, pus spots or swelling.

viva.q: What do you look for inside the nose?
viva.a: Discharge, bleeding, a bent partition and swollen ridges, which point to infection, allergy or blockage.

viva.q: Why press over the cheek and forehead?
viva.a: Tenderness there suggests sinus infection in an older child who can report pain.

viva.q: What do you note about the tonsils and throat?
viva.a: Size, redness, pus spots and throat redness, which explain sore throat, fever and snoring.

title.en: Inspection of breathing and the chest

items.summary: Watching the rate, pattern and effort of breathing, the shape and symmetry of the chest wall, and the movement of each zone.

blocks.title: Breathing pattern
bullets: Count the breaths and note whether the rhythm stays even or turns uneven.
Note whether the belly, the chest or both move with each breath.
Listen without any instrument for grunting, harsh in-breath noise or wheeze.

blocks.title: Chest shape and surface
bullets: Stand back and compare the left and right sides for equal shape.
Look at the midline cord in the neck and see if it drifts to either side.
Look for straining neck muscles, widening nostrils and ribs sucking inward.
Find where the strongest beat shows, normally the fourth rib gap inside the nipple line.
Look for a drooped shoulder, hollows above or below the collarbone, wasting below the shoulder blade and crowded ribs.
Check the backbone runs straight without a sideways or forward bend.
Look for scars, discharging openings, full surface veins and throbbing spots.

blocks.title: Movement
bullets: Watch every zone on both sides: above and below the collarbone, breast and below it, armpit and below it.
Watch above, between and below the shoulder blades on the back.
Name any zone where movement looks smaller than its match.

viva.q: Where is the strongest beat normally seen in a small child?
viva.a: In the fourth rib gap, just inside the nipple line on the left side.

viva.q: What effort signs do you watch for?
viva.a: Straining neck muscles, widening nostrils, ribs sucking in and uneven rhythm.

viva.q: Why compare matching zones on both sides?
viva.a: One sided poor movement points to fluid, air, solid lung or shrinkage on that side.

title.en: Palpation of the chest and its measurements

items.summary: Feeling the windpipe position, the strongest beat, chest movement and voice vibration, plus simple tape measurements of the chest.

blocks.title: What to feel
bullets: Confirm the windpipe sits midline or has shifted, using the dip above the breastbone.
Confirm the strongest beat in the fourth rib gap inside the nipple line and note if it feels spread out.
Compare movement on both sides zone by zone as the child breathes.
Feel voice vibration while the child chants ninety nine and note weaker patches.
Press the bones and rib gaps for soreness.
Feel for a grating rub, a wheeze buzz or a crackle buzz on the wall.

blocks.title: Measurements
bullets: Record the front to back and side to side diameters in centimetres.
Record the tape distance round the chest at nipple level.
Record how much the chest widens on a deep breath, usually 2 to 5 centimetres.
Record each half of the chest and how much each side widens.

viva.q: How do you test voice vibration on the wall?
viva.a: Ask the child to chant ninety nine while your palm feels each zone for equal buzz.

viva.q: What is the usual chest widening on deep breathing?
viva.a: About 2 to 5 centimetres in a healthy child.

viva.q: What does a shifted windpipe tell you?
viva.a: Fluid or air pushes it away, while shrinkage and scarring pull it closer.

title.en: Percussion of the chest and how to tap correctly

items.summary: Tapping each chest zone for its note, marking the liver and heart edges, and the tapping method examiners watch closely.

blocks.title: What to percuss
bullets: Tap every zone on the front, side and back, grading the note as ringing, dulled, extra ringing, flat or stony flat.
Mark where the liver starts, usually at the right fifth rib gap, and note its length in centimetres.
Match the left heart edge to the strongest beat and the right edge to the side of the breastbone.
Keep shifting dullness, tidal tapping and the Traube area for cases where they are indicated.

blocks.title: Tapping method
bullets: Lay the middle finger of the weaker hand flat on the chest as the base plate.
Strike it with the tip of the stronger middle or index finger.
Keep the base finger parallel to any dull edge being mapped.
Lift the other fingers off the wall so the sound is not muffled.
Let the strike spring from the wrist joint.
Lift the striking finger at once so the note can ring out.
Tap the collarbone directly without a base finger.
Move from ringing zones toward dull zones.
Always match each spot with the same spot on the other side.
Rest hands on the head for the armpit and cross arms to the far shoulders for the back.

viva.q: Which finger strikes and which receives?
viva.a: The stronger middle or index finger strikes the middle finger of the weaker hand.

viva.q: Why move from ringing toward dull areas?
viva.a: The change in note is heard more clearly when approached from the ringing side.

viva.q: How do you position the child for the side and back?
viva.a: Hands on the head for the armpit, arms crossed to the far shoulders for the back.

title.en: Listening to the lungs and voice sounds

items.summary: Where to place the stethoscope on a child, and how to judge breath sounds, added sounds and the conduction of the voice.

blocks.title: Coverage
blocks.text: Listen down the front from above the collarbone to the sixth rib, down the side from the armpit to the eighth rib, and down the back to the eleventh rib, always matching each spot with the other side.

blocks.title: What to judge
bullets: Name the breath sound as soft and airy, harsh and tubular, or mixed.
Grade the loudness in each zone as normal, faint or harsh.
Note crackles, wheezes or a friction rub and the exact zone where they sit.
Test voice conduction and note normal, louder or fainter patches, including false signs such as clear numbers, audible whispers or bleating.
Add the coin test or the splash test when air and fluid are suspected together.

viva.q: How far down do you listen on the back?
viva.a: Down to the eleventh rib, comparing each level with the other side.

viva.q: What added sounds must you name with their site?
viva.a: Crackles, wheezes and friction rubs, each tied to the zone where heard.

viva.q: When do you use the coin or splash test?
viva.a: When air and fluid together are suspected in the chest cavity.

title.en: Words for difficult and noisy breathing

items.summary: Six bedside words examiners expect: grunting, deep or shallow breathing, breathlessness, and breathlessness tied to posture.

head: Term
What it means
rows: Noisy out-breath through a half shut voice box that holds pressure in the air sacs
Breathing that runs deeper than normal
Breathing that runs shallower than normal
Breathlessness that worsens when lying flat
Breathlessness that worsens when sitting or standing

viva.q: What is a grunt doing for the baby?
viva.a: The half shut voice box traps pressure at the end of each breath to keep air sacs open.

viva.q: How do orthopnoea and platypnoea differ?
viva.a: One worsens lying flat, the other worsens upright, pointing to different causes.

title.en: What common chest signs point to

items.summary: How the position of the windpipe, the tapping note, breath sounds and voice tests narrow down the likely chest cause.

blocks.title: Windpipe position
bullets: Fluid, pus, trapped air, or air with fluid together push the windpipe to the far side.
Solid lung, over expanded lung, wide airway disease and asthma leave it central.
Shrunken and scarred lung pull it toward the same side.

blocks.title: Tapping note
bullets: Extra ringing sits over trapped air around the lung.
Normal ringing belongs to a healthy chest.
Dulling sits over solid, shrunken or scarred lung.
Stony flatness sits over fluid, very large solid patches and solid growths.

blocks.title: Breath and voice sounds
bullets: Soft airy sounds are the normal pattern.
Harsh tubular sounds sit over solid or shrunken lung.
Mixed sounds are heard in asthma and in over expanded lungs.
Voice vibration and voice echo rise over solid lung.
They fall or vanish with fluid, trapped air, shrinkage, scarring, pus, air with fluid, and asthma.

viva.q: Name causes that push the windpipe away.
viva.a: Fluid, pus, trapped air, or air with fluid together on one side of the chest.

viva.q: What note do you expect over a pleural effusion?
viva.a: A stony flat note with lost voice vibration and echo on that side.

viva.q: What sounds sit over consolidation?
viva.a: Harsh tubular breathing with louder voice echo and a dulled tapping note.
